blocks.title: Deployment and Beyond
blocks.body:
Deploying an AI system is not the end of the responsible AI journey - it is the beginning of an ongoing process of oversight, monitoring and governance. AI systems can behave differently in the real world than in testing. Data drifts, contexts change, and biases that were not apparent during development can emerge at scale.

This stage also covers what happens when the AI lifecycle ends - how systems are decommissioned, decisions documented, and accountability maintained over time.

blocks.title: If you use AI tools rather than build them
blocks.body: At the deployment stage, you're often the sensor no automated monitoring system can replace: if an AI tool's output looks off, unexpected, or unfair, you may be the first person to notice. Report it through whatever feedback channel your organisation provides - don't assume someone else will catch it - and don't forward or act on output you haven't verified just because it came from a tool your organisation has already approved. Being the human in the loop is a real responsibility, not a formality.

blocks.title: The frameworks suggest...
blocks.body:
The EU AI Act requires providers of high-risk AI systems to implement post-market monitoring plans, collecting and reviewing performance data in real-world conditions and taking corrective action where problems are identified.

The ICO's AI and Data Protection Risk Toolkit provides practical guidance for organisations on auditing AI systems and ensuring compliance with data protection law throughout deployment - including tools for assessing automated decision-making and its impact on individuals.

items.title: Fair access and responsible release
items.body: Launch is itself an ethical moment, not just an operational one. A staged rollout - a small, representative pilot group before a full release - lets you catch problems before they scale, but only if 'small' doesn't mean 'the easiest users to reach': a pilot skewed toward existing power users or one demographic can miss exactly the harms it needs to catch. How a new AI feature is announced matters too - users should be told what it does, what it doesn't do, and how to get help or opt out, not left to discover an AI system through its mistakes.

items.title: Monitoring for bias drift
items.body: AI systems can develop new biases over time as the data they process changes. A model trained on pre-pandemic data may behave differently in a post-pandemic world. Ongoing monitoring - testing for changes in performance across different groups - is an essential part of responsible deployment.

items.title: Human oversight
items.body: Responsible AI does not mean replacing human judgement - it means augmenting it thoughtfully. High-stakes AI decisions should include a mechanism for human review, particularly where errors could cause serious harm: in healthcare, criminal justice, credit decisions and employment. This oversight fails more often through automation bias - a reviewer trusting the AI's output more than the evidence warrants, and rubber-stamping it - than through the review step being missing altogether. A human in the loop only provides real oversight if they have the time, information and standing to actually disagree with the system, not just to approve it.

items.title: Feedback mechanisms
items.body: Users and those affected by AI decisions should have a way to flag concerns, challenge decisions and seek redress. Where a decision is solely automated, this is more than good practice - UK and EU GDPR give people a legal right to contest it and request meaningful human review. Contestability isn't a feedback form bolted on after launch; it's a design requirement, built in from the start, that someone can say a decision was wrong and have a real person able to act on that.

items.title: Planning for when things go wrong
items.body: Twitter and Replit, both covered below, only worked out how to communicate about their failures after the failure was already public. A pre-agreed plan - who speaks, what gets disclosed, how quickly, and to whom - turns an incident into a demonstration of accountability rather than a second, slower-moving crisis. This is worth deciding in advance, not improvising under pressure.

items.title: Decommissioning
items.body: When an AI system is retired, responsible practice requires documentation - such as an updated model card - recording the system's use, known limitations and any incidents. Public registers exist for some AI - the UK's Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard (ATRS) for public-sector use, and the EU's public database for high-risk systems under the AI Act - but most private-sector AI has no public register to submit to. For everything else, the equivalent is keeping your organisation's internal AI system inventory up to date, including systems that have been retired (see Operationalising Responsible AI).

blocks.title: AI governance structures
blocks.body:
Responsible AI requires deliberate governance structures - the accountability, oversight and decision-making processes needed to embed ethical AI practice across an organisation.

Key components include: clear AI policies and principles; an AI ethics committee or working group; a risk assessment and management process; an inventory of AI systems in use; monitoring and auditing tools; and training and enablement for staff.

ISO 42001 provides a structured framework for implementing these components. The ICO's AI and Data Protection Risk Toolkit provides practical audit tools aligned with UK data protection law.

blocks.title: Case study: Twitter's image cropping algorithm
blocks.body:
From 2018 to 2021, Twitter used an AI algorithm to automatically crop images shown in timelines. The algorithm was trained to focus on the most visually 'salient' part of an image. Twitter said at the time that it had tested the algorithm for racial and gender bias before launch and found none.

In 2020, users began reporting that the algorithm nonetheless consistently cropped to lighter-skinned faces when images included people of different ethnicities. Twitter's own follow-up analysis, published in 2021, confirmed both a racial and gender bias in the cropping behaviour.

The lesson isn't that testing didn't happen - it's that the pre-launch testing wasn't rigorous or representative enough to catch the disparity, and post-launch monitoring didn't catch it either; it took users noticing the pattern themselves before the company investigated further. Twitter discontinued the feature in 2021, concluding that deciding how to crop an image is a decision better made by people than by an algorithm - acknowledging the bias had operated, at scale, for three years before it was addressed.

Source: Twitter Engineering: Sharing learnings about our image cropping algorithm (2021)

blocks.title: What would have caught Twitter's cropping bias sooner?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: Rolling the new cropping feature out far more gradually, to a smaller group of users at first.
items.feedback: Not quite. A slower rollout delays the problem but doesn't detect it - without monitoring for demographic bias, the same issue would likely have surfaced eventually regardless of rollout speed.

items.text: Building the cropping feature on a more technically sophisticated AI model overall.
items.feedback: Not quite. The bias wasn't caused by the model being unsophisticated - it came from what the model was trained to prioritise. A more advanced model could easily carry the same bias.

items.text: Monitoring outcomes across demographic groups after launch, backed by a user feedback channel.
Replacing the automated cropping entirely with manual review carried out by staff.
items.feedback: Not quite. Manual review at Twitter's scale isn't realistic, and it doesn't address the underlying question of how the automated system's bias should have been caught in the first place.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Twitter did test before launch and found no bias - but that testing wasn't rigorous or representative enough to catch it. The bias was eventually detected only when users noticed the pattern themselves. More representative pre-launch testing, combined with a formal post-launch monitoring programme and a structured feedback mechanism, would have surfaced the problem far sooner than three years after deployment.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. Twitter did test for bias before launch, but that testing wasn't rigorous or representative enough to catch it, and the bias went undetected until users noticed the pattern themselves. More representative pre-launch testing, combined with post-launch monitoring and a real feedback mechanism, would have caught it far sooner.

blocks.title: Case study: An AI coding agent deletes a live database
blocks.body:
The case studies so far all involve predictive AI - systems that score, rank or classify, leaving a person to act on the output. Agentic AI raises a distinct risk: the system doesn't just recommend an action, it carries the action out itself. Security researchers have a name for this specific failure mode - the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (covered on the Modeling page) calls it Excessive Agency: an AI system able to take actions beyond what it was actually authorised to do.

In July 2025, a startup founder used an AI coding agent, built into the Replit platform, to help build and manage a software project - instructing it explicitly, in writing and more than once, not to make any changes to the live system without asking first, including an active code freeze. Despite those instructions, the agent went on to run commands that deleted the project's production database. When the founder - Jason Lemkin of SaaStr - asked whether the damage could be undone, the agent claimed the deletion was irreversible; that claim turned out to be false, and Lemkin recovered the data himself.

Replit's CEO, Amjad Masad, publicly acknowledged the incident and apologised, and the company announced changes intended to prevent a recurrence - including separating development and production databases by default, a planning-only mode that separates an agent's 'planning' from its ability to actually execute changes, and an improved one-click backup restore.

Source: The Register: Replit makes vibe-y promise to stop its AI agents making vibe coding disasters (2025)

blocks.title: What was the core problem behind the database deletion?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: The AI agent had been trained on biased data, which led it to make a poor decision.
items.feedback: Not quite. This wasn't a case of biased training data producing a skewed judgement call - the agent ran destructive commands it was explicitly told not to run, then denied it could reverse them.

items.text: The agent could act beyond the limits it was given, then misreported what it had done.
The company had never signed a data processing agreement with its AI vendor.
items.feedback: Not quite. The case doesn't turn on contracts or data processing agreements - the core failure was the agent acting beyond its authorised boundaries and misreporting the consequences.

items.text: The underlying AI model simply wasn't accurate enough for production use.
items.feedback: Not quite. Accuracy wasn't the issue here - even a highly accurate agent can still take actions it wasn't authorised to take, which is exactly what 'excessive agency' means.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is what makes agentic AI a distinct category of risk, rather than just another predictive model: the system can take real, irreversible actions in the world - not just produce output for a person to review - and can act outside the boundaries it was explicitly given, then misreport its own behaviour. This is named Excessive Agency in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications. Human oversight has to cover what an AI agent is capable of doing, not just what it is asked to do, with permissions and safeguards (such as backups, and separating planning from execution) designed accordingly.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The core issue here isn't data bias, contracts or accuracy - it's that the agent could autonomously execute real, destructive actions beyond the boundaries it had explicitly been given, and then misrepresented what it had done. That's the defining risk of agentic AI: oversight has to cover what a system is capable of doing, not just what it's told to do.

blocks.title: Case study: An airline's chatbot invents its own refund policy
blocks.body:
Not every AI failure involves prediction or agency - sometimes it's simpler than that: a generative AI chatbot confidently gets a fact wrong, and the company deploying it is held responsible for what it said.

In 2022, a customer asked Air Canada's website chatbot about bereavement fares after a family member's death. The chatbot told him he could apply for the discount retroactively, within 90 days of travel. That was wrong - Air Canada's actual policy required the request to be made before travel - but he booked in reliance on what the chatbot told him, and the airline later refused to honour it, arguing the chatbot was 'a separate legal entity responsible for its own actions'.

In February 2024, Canada's Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected that argument and found Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation. The tribunal was blunt: a company is responsible for all the information on its website, 'whether it comes from a static page or a chatbot' - it makes no difference that a generative AI tool, not a person, produced the wrong answer.

Source: Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149

blocks.title: What does the Air Canada case establish about AI chatbots?
blocks.instruction: Select one option, then select Submit.

items.text: An organisation isn't responsible for what its own chatbot tells a customer, since the AI generated the answer itself.
items.feedback: Not quite. The tribunal specifically rejected this argument - Air Canada was found liable for its chatbot's incorrect statement, just as it would be for any other information on its own website.

items.text: An organisation is responsible for the information its chatbot gives customers, even where the chatbot generated it independently.
The case turned on whether the chatbot's underlying AI model was defective or poorly trained.
items.feedback: Not quite. The tribunal didn't need to examine why the chatbot got it wrong - what mattered was that the airline presented the chatbot's answer as reliable information, and a customer relied on it.

items.text: Bereavement fares are not something airlines can legally offer through an automated tool.
items.feedback: Not quite. This case wasn't about whether bereavement fares can be handled by an automated tool - it was about accountability for what the tool said, once it said something wrong.

blocks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The tribunal held that a company is responsible for all the information on its website, "whether it comes from a static page or a chatbot". Deploying a generative AI tool doesn't create a liability shield - an organisation remains accountable for what it tells customers, regardless of what produced the answer.
blocks.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite. The tribunal ruled that a company is responsible for information on its website "whether it comes from a static page or a chatbot" - deploying an AI tool doesn't let an organisation disclaim what it told a customer.

blocks.title: Coming up...
blocks.body: You've now followed the full AI lifecycle through an ethical lens. In the Conclusion, we'll bring together the guiding principles, reflect on your individual role in responsible AI, and share practical top tips to take into your work.
